\begin{document}

\title{Don't Reweight, Calibrate: Per-Label Class Weights Distort Top-$K$ Ranking and Prior-Fallback Calibration Repairs It}

\author{Akifumi Goto}
\email{souldrive7@gmail.com}
\affiliation{\institution{Independent researcher}\country{Japan}}

\begin{abstract}
Systems that rank $L$ labels per row (a customer's next product, a document's tags) routinely train one-vs-rest models with a label-specific positive-class weight such as \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}$=n_-/n_+$ to counter imbalance. The textbook account of the consequence is Elkan's identity: a weight $w_j$ shifts label $j$'s log-odds by $\ln w_j$, so the model ranks by $w_j\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij})$ instead of the marginal $p_{ij}$ that is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and the shift can be undone analytically. Whether that account describes what a finite learner does with weights in the thousands or millions, and which post-hoc repair then works, has not been measured on a top-$K$ benchmark. On the Santander product-recommendation benchmark (\nnTest{} test rows, \nnLabels{} labels), for two LightGBM rankers that differ only in the weights, we decompose the top-$K$ loss with a what-if device, an analytic inversion, and a ladder of post-hoc repairs. The ideal odds shift explains \noddsShare\% of the loss; the rest is a per-label monotone distortion, mostly a constant logit shift that differs from $\ln w_j$ plus ties from leaf saturation, which the inversion cannot undo but per-label calibration can, provided that labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior: $\mapseven$ goes from $\nNraw$ (unweighted) to $\nSraw$ (weighted) and to $\nSplIsoPrior$ after per-label isotonic regression, within $\nSplIsoPriorCeilGap$ of the in-sample ceiling, and the repair survives a deployment protocol that calibrates on the training period. Dose-response experiments on \nnMulan{} MULAN benchmarks with \nnLearners{} learners and a synthetic study with known marginals reproduce the odds shift, its exact inversion under a realizable learner, its failure under leaf saturation (which LightGBM shows at every tree count we tried and XGBoost with its default regularization does not), and the harm of per-label calibration when calibration positives are scarce; selecting among per-label maps with a positives threshold, a shared map and no calibration by cross-validation inside the calibration split removes that harm on every benchmark for the default learner. The recommendation is to estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss, calibrate with a fallback and a selection rule fixed on the calibration split, and decide at top-$K$.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ranking many binary labels within a row is the operational core of product recommendation, tagging, and risk triage: for each customer the system scores every product, sorts, and shows the top $K$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Menon2019Reductions}. The labels are almost always imbalanced, and the most common remedy in gradient-boosting practice is a per-label positive-class weight, \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight} in XGBoost and LightGBM~\cite{Chen2016XGBoost,Ke2017LightGBM}, for which the XGBoost documentation suggests $n_-/n_+$~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; the same recipe is \texttt{pos\_weight} in binary cross-entropy for neural multi-label models.

Label-specific weights are not a free choice when the deliverable is a per-row ranking. Two facts are classical. Ranking labels by their marginal $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and one-vs-rest training with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Menon2019Reductions,Wydmuch2018PLT}. A positive-class weight $w$ moves the population minimizer of a proper loss from $p$ to $wp/(wp+1-p)$, an odds shift by $w$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}. Together they say that a label-specific $w_j$ makes the model rank by $w_j\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij})$, a different ranking whenever the weights differ, and the XGBoost documentation itself warns that a re-balanced model no longer predicts the right probability~\cite{XGBoostDocs}.

What the classical account leaves open is what a finite learner does when $w_j$ is in the thousands or millions, as the recommended value is for rare labels, and which post-hoc repair then works. Long-tailed recognition has reached the analogous conclusion for classification, that adjusting the classifier after unweighted training beats re-weighting the loss~\cite{Kang2020Decoupling,Menon2021LogitAdjust}, and label-shift adaptation combines calibration with a prior correction~\cite{Lipton2018LabelShift,Alexandari2020MLLS}; but both lines rank classes within one softmax, not labels across independent one-vs-rest models. Per-label isotonic regression is known to break top-$k$ accuracy in multi-class settings~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, and the extreme multi-label literature deliberately uses one shared monotone map so that precision@$k$ is untouched, deferring per-label calibration to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}. Neither line measures the cross-label consequence of training weights on a top-$K$ benchmark, nor the role of the calibrator's behaviour on labels that have no calibration positives.

\Cref{fig:one} gives our answer on the Santander benchmark, on a pair of LightGBM models that differ only in the weights. Applying the ideal odds shift to the unweighted model predicts a fraction of the loss that the trained weighted model actually suffers; the remainder is a per-label monotone distortion, mostly a constant logit shift that differs from $\ln w_j$, plus ties created by leaf saturation (\cref{lem:leaf}); the analytic inversion cannot undo it, and per-label calibration repairs it up to a small residue above the in-sample ceiling. The repair holds under a deployment protocol that calibrates on the training period, and it depends on one implementation detail: a label without calibration positives must be mapped to its prior, not passed through, otherwise the untouched labels occupy the top of every row (\cref{prop:dead}).

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Where the textbook account stops.} Using Elkan's identity as a what-if device we separate the top-$K$ loss of a weighted ranker into the ideal odds shift, a further per-label monotone distortion, and a residue above the in-sample per-label ceiling (\cref{fig:one}A, \cref{tab:ladder}). On Santander, for two LightGBM models that differ only in the weights, the shift is \noddsShare\% of the loss; the rest is mostly a per-label constant that differs from $\ln w_j$ (\cref{fig:two}), with ties from leaf saturation (\cref{lem:leaf}) above the ceiling. Capping the leaf step (\texttt{max\_delta\_step}) removes the saturation and most of the raw loss, yet the analytic inversion still does not help, because the realized shift is then smaller than $\ln w_j$; per-label calibration does (\cref{tab:mds}).
\item \textbf{Per-label calibration with a prior fallback is the repair.} With labels without calibration positives mapped to their prior, per-label isotonic regression is the best post-hoc repair on all three Santander base models, within $0.01$ of the in-sample per-label ceiling, under the test-split protocol and under a deployment protocol that calibrates on the training period (\cref{tab:ladder}, \cref{tab:deploy}); a shared map never inverts a pair and repairs nothing beyond tie resolution (\cref{rem:shared}). The fallback policy is not a detail: with the identity fallback the same calibrator lowers a direct-probability model below its raw score (\cref{fig:one}B, \cref{prop:dead}). On Santander the median calibrated label has \ncalPosMedAlive{} calibration positives, so the comparison isolates the policy from small-sample error for all but the rarest labels.
\item \textbf{Dose-response and a recipe with its selection rule.} Across \nnMulan{} MULAN benchmarks, \nnLearners{} learners and a synthetic study with known marginals, the odds shift appears for every learner as \cref{prop:odds} predicts and is exactly invertible for a realizable learner, the inversion fails once the learner saturates, and per-label calibration with the prior fallback \emph{hurts} an unweighted model where calibration positives are scarce (\cref{tab:mulan}, \cref{app:mulan,app:synthetic}). The recipe is therefore conditional: unweighted proper loss, then per-label calibration with a positives threshold, a shared map, or no calibration, the choice made by cross-validation \emph{inside} the calibration split, then decision at top-$K$. The selection removes the significant harm of the default learner on every MULAN dataset (\cref{tab:tau}) but fails on the smallest calibration split, and a size sweep on Santander gives the split size below which per-label maps lose to the shared map on an unweighted model, while they win at every size on the weighted one (\cref{tab:calsize}).
\end{enumerate}
All numbers are generated by one script from result files released with the paper; the dead-label policy of every calibrator is explicit.

\section{Setup and Theory}
\label{sec:theory}

Rows $i=1,\dots,n$ carry features $x_i$ and binary labels $y_{ij}$, $j=1,\dots,L$; $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is the marginal and $\pi_j=\Pr(y_{ij}=1)$ the prevalence. A scorer returns $s_{ij}$ and the system shows the $K$ largest scores of row $i$. We evaluate with $\mapk$ in the Kaggle definition (average precision at $K$ per row, averaged over rows with at least one positive) and report per-row bootstrap intervals. For precision@$K$ the population-optimal ranking sorts by $p_{ij}$, and one-vs-rest with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Koyejo2015Consistent,Menon2019Reductions}. A post-hoc calibrator is \emph{separable} if it maps label $j$ by a non-decreasing $g_j$ independently of the other labels; per-label Platt, isotonic, temperature and beta calibration~\cite{Platt1999,Zadrozny2002,Guo2017Calibration,Kull2017Beta} are separable, and so is the shared (pooled) isotonic map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} with $g_j\equiv g$. A positive-class weight $w_j>0$ multiplies the loss of the positives of label $j$ (\texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, \texttt{pos\_weight}).

\begin{remark}[Shared maps never invert, distinct maps can]
\label{rem:shared}
If $g_1=\dots=g_L$ the calibrator never creates a strict inversion within a row, so a shared map is rank-neutral up to ties and can repair nothing beyond tie resolution. If two continuous maps differ at an interior point, some row's strict order is inverted. Both halves are folklore (\cref{app:proof}); shared class-wise binning~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, intra-order-preserving maps~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} and the shared map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} rely on the first. A per-label map can reorder, and in the population limit it should: calibrated per-label maps return the marginals. Per-label calibration therefore hurts only through estimation error, whose boundary case is a label without calibration positives (\cref{prop:dead}).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Odds shift, after Elkan]
\label{prop:odds}
Let $q_{ij}$ be the population minimizer of a strictly proper binary loss with positive-class weight $w_j$. Then $\operatorname{logit}q_{ij}=\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}+\ln w_j$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}, and for $p_{ij}>p_{ik}$ the weighted scores reverse the pair iff $\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}-\operatorname{logit}p_{ik}<\ln w_k-\ln w_j$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The weighted loss is the unweighted loss under the tilted distribution whose posterior odds are $w_j$ times the original; the flip condition is the difference of the shifted logits.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:odds}
(a) A common weight $w_j\equiv w$ is a shared map and never changes within-row order. (b) The flipped pairs, hence the top-$K$ loss of the \emph{ideal} weighted model, depend only on the unweighted logit gaps and the intended weights, so they can be computed from an unweighted model before weighted training (\emph{what-if}); this describes a learner that realizes the shift exactly, not necessarily the one a finite learner produces. (c) When $w_jp_{ij}\ll1$, $q_{ij}\approx w_jp_{ij}$, so weighted training approximates the optimal ranking for a propensity-weighted precision@$K$ with propensities $1/w_j$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Wydmuch2021PSPLT}: training weights silently change the metric. If a utility-weighted ranking is wanted, multiplying calibrated marginals by the utilities is exact.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Leaf saturation]
\label{lem:leaf}
For weighted log-loss the optimal constant in a tree leaf with $n_+$ positives and $n_-$ negatives is $\rho(w)=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$. Any leaf with $n_+\ge1$ satisfies $\rho(w)\ge1-n_-/(wn_+)$, so its prediction is within $\varepsilon$ of one once $w\ge n_-/(\varepsilon n_+)$; all test cells routed to such leaves tie near one and lose their order across those leaves.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$-wn_+\ln\rho-n_-\ln(1-\rho)$ is minimized at $\rho=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$, and $1-\rho=n_-/(wn_++n_-)\le n_-/(wn_+)$.
\end{proof}

The lemma is exact for a single tree whose leaf values are weighted class frequencies and describes the fixed point that a boosted ensemble approaches when it fits the weighted objective well; it is the tree analogue of importance weights losing their effect on a flexible learner~\cite{Byrd2019}. With the recommended $w_j\approx1/\pi_j$ and leaves of at most $m$ negatives, every positive-containing leaf of a label with $\pi_j\le\varepsilon/m$ is within $\varepsilon$ of one. Two consequences follow and should be kept apart. The realized shift is no longer the constant $\ln w_j$ of \cref{prop:odds}, so the analytic inversion $q\mapsto q/(q+w(1-q))$ stops working, but the distortion is still monotone within each label, so a per-label monotone map fitted on calibration data can undo it. And the cells tied at one within a label have lost their mutual order, which no separable map recovers; this part is bounded by the gap between the in-sample per-label ceiling and the unweighted model.

\begin{remark}[Dead-label takeover]
\label{prop:dead}
Let label $d$ have no calibration positives and keep its raw score $s_{id}$ (identity fallback), while every calibrated label $j$ is mapped by $g_j$ with $g_j(s)\le\bar q$ for all $s$ (isotonic outputs are bounded by the largest block mean of the calibration split). If $s_{id}>\bar q$ then $d$ is ranked above every calibrated label in row $i$ regardless of $y_{id}$; with $m$ such labels, $m$ of the top-$K$ slots are occupied by them. The condition holds whenever raw scores are inflated relative to calibrated ones, which is the situation that motivates calibration. This is an implementation pitfall, not a property of standard libraries: of \nnSurveyImpl{} calibration implementations we examined (scikit-learn, netcal, PyCalib, MAPIE, torch-uncertainty, betacal, venn-abers, the released code of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib,Patel2021IMax}), every one-vs-rest calibrator returns a constant or raises on a single-class split, and only MAPIE's top-label calibrator passes an unseen label through, with a warning. Our own earlier one-vs-rest loop, and any loop that catches the failure and returns the input, produces the takeover. Dead labels themselves are not exotic: a random calibration split of \ndeadFreqSantOnePctNcal{} Santander test rows leaves \ndeadFreqSantOnePct{} of \nnLabels{} labels without a positive on average, and the 30\% split leaves \ndeadFreqMedicalThirty{} of \nmedL{} on MULAN medical. A prior fallback ($\tilde s_{id}=\hat\pi_d$) or exclusion removes the effect; the policy should be an explicit argument of the calibrator.
\end{remark}

\label{sec:santander}

\paragraph{Data and models.} The Santander Product Recommendation data~\cite{KaggleSantander2016} has \nnLabels{} products; we use the public time split with \nnTrain{} training rows, \nnValRows{} validation rows (the last training months) and \nnTest{} test rows, and the Kaggle $\mapseven$. Three base scorers produce test probabilities for every cell. \Sm and \Nm are LightGBM one-vs-rest models trained by one script in one session with \emph{identical} configuration (60 trees, learning rate $0.05$, 31 leaves, no feature or row subsampling, one seed, the same feature pipeline and split); the only difference is that \Sm sets $w_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$ per label (between \nwMin{} and \nwMax) and \Nm sets no weight. An earlier run of the weighted configuration (\cref{tab:mds}) differs from \Sm by $\nSorigMinusS$ in raw $\mapseven$ and behaves the same on every rung. \Wm (Wasserstein gradient boosting, WGBoost~\cite{Matsubara2024WGBoost}) estimates Beta-distributed probabilities directly without weights. A fourth scorer, \Nhm, is an earlier unweighted LightGBM run with 100 trees and feature and row subsampling; it is reported as a robustness column. Two calibration protocols are used. The \emph{test-split} protocol fits calibrators on a random 30\% of the test rows (seed 42, \nnVal{} rows) and evaluates on the remaining 70\%; it is optimistic for deployment because the calibration rows come from the test period, and its gain on the unweighted model ($\nciNprior$) bounds what the protocol itself contributes. The \emph{deployment} protocol fits calibrators on the validation period and evaluates on all test rows (\cref{tab:deploy}). Under the test-split protocol \nSnDead{} labels have no positives in the calibration split and every calibrated label has at least \ncalPosMinAlive{} (median \ncalPosMedAlive). Bootstrap intervals use $B=\nbootB$ per-row resamples of the \nbootN{} evaluation rows with a positive.

\paragraph{Decomposition and repair ladder (\cref{fig:one}, \cref{tab:ladder}).} The weighted model loses $\nSloss$ $\mapseven$ against \Nm; we express every repair as the share of this loss it returns. Adding $\ln w_j$ to the logits of \Nm is the ideal weighted model of \cref{prop:odds}; it scores $\nwhatifIdeal$, changes the top-7 set of \nfracRowsChangedWhatif\% of the first $500{,}000$ rows while keeping \noverlapWhatif{} of 7 items, and accounts for \noddsShare\% of the loss (with the milder $\sqrt{w_j}$ the ideal model scores $\nwhatifHalf$, so a weaker weight shrinks this part, though we did not train such a model). The trained \Sm keeps only \noverlapS{} of 7 items, has \nSsatOne\% of its cells at exactly $1.0$ and \nSsatZero\% at exactly $0.0$, and the analytic inversion with the known $w_j$ returns \nelkanShare\% ($\nSelkan$). The remaining distortion is per-label and monotone, and the ladder measures its shape by what each repair reaches. An intercept-only logit shift fitted per label on the calibration split returns \noffsetShare\% ($\nSplOffsetPrior$), so for most labels the realized distortion is close to a constant, but not the constant $\ln w_j$; \cref{fig:two} shows why label by label: the label-free prevalence-matching shift $b_j$ equals $\ln w_j$ for the labels whose cells never saturate, exactly as \cref{prop:odds} says, and for every other label the cells at exactly $1.0$ cannot be moved by a finite shift, so $b_j$ jumps to the clipping bound or is unreachable (\nnCappedShift{} labels). Per-label Platt scaling~\cite{Platt1999} returns \nplattShare\% and beta calibration~\cite{Kull2017Beta} \nbetaShare\%; per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback returns \nrepairShare\% ($\nSplIsoPrior$, i.e.\ \nrepairExtraShare\% beyond the odds shift), within $\nSplIsoPriorCeilGap$ of the in-sample per-label ceiling ($\nSceil$); the remaining \ntieShare\% ($\nSceilGap$) lies above that ceiling, and the cells tied at exactly $1.0$ or $0.0$ are its visible cause (\cref{lem:leaf}). The bootstrap difference between \Nm raw and the repaired \Sm is $\nciNminusS$; under the same calibrator \Nm itself reaches $\nNplIsoPrior$, so the like-for-like gap is $\nNplIsoPrior-\nSplIsoPrior$. Two symptoms agree: the mean within-label AUC (200{,}000-row subsample), which no monotone map can change, is $\nNauc$ for \Nm and $\nSauc$ for \Sm, and the ceiling of \Sm ($\nSceil$) sits against the raw $\nNraw$ of \Nm. Pooled isotonic leaves \Wm and \Nm unchanged, as \cref{rem:shared} requires, and moves \Sm from $\nSraw$ to $\nSpooled$ only because pooled blocks merge the tied cells and the stable sort breaks ties by label index; no strictly ordered pair is inverted. The earlier run \Nhm (100 trees, subsampling) behaves like \Nm on every rung (\cref{tab:ladder}), so the decomposition does not hinge on the control's capacity. Capping the leaf step changes the picture at training time (\cref{tab:mds}): with \texttt{max\_delta\_step}$=0.7$ the weighted model has \nSmdsasatOne\% of cells at exactly $1.0$ and scores $\nSmdsaraw$ raw, with $2$ it has \nSmdsbsatOne\% and scores $\nSmdsbraw$, close to the unweighted $\nNraw$; but the analytic inversion now \emph{lowers} both ($\nSmdsaelkan$ and $\nSmdsbelkan$), because the cap keeps the realized shift below $\ln w_j$ and the inversion over-corrects, whereas per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback reaches $\nSmdsaplIsoPrior$ and $\nSmdsbplIsoPrior$, the latter above the unweighted raw score. The inversion therefore fails for two reasons that the sweep separates: saturation ties without a cap, and an under-realized shift with one; a per-label monotone map handles both.

\paragraph{The fallback decides the sign.} With the identity fallback, per-label isotonic regression yields $\nSplIsoId$ on \Sm (\nSplIsoIdRel\% relative to raw, below the popularity baseline: $\nciSidMinusPop$ against $\npopMAP$) and lowers \Wm from $\nWraw$ to $\nWplIsoId$ (\nWplIsoIdRel\%): the \nSnDead{} dead labels keep their raw scores (mean $\nWdeadRawMean$ on \Wm) while every calibrated label shrinks to its prevalence (largest mean $\nWaliveCalMax$), so all three sit in the top 7 of \nWdeadAllRowsPct\% of rows, the takeover of \cref{prop:dead}. This is a pitfall of the calibration wrapper, not of isotonic regression; we report it because the same wrapper produced a published negative result of ours, and because \cref{sec:dose} shows that scarce calibration positives hurt even with the prior fallback, so the two effects must be kept apart. With the prior fallback the same calibrator gives $\nSplIsoPrior$ on \Sm, $\nWplIsoPrior$ on \Wm (\nWplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciWprior$) and $\nNplIsoPrior$ on \Nm (\nNplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciNprior$), each within $0.01$ of its ceiling ($\nSceil$, $\nWceil$, $\nNceil$); exclusion behaves like the prior. The \nSnDead{} dead labels also have no positives in the evaluation split (\nnDeadTest{} labels have none), so the prior costs nothing here; on data where a label is rare in the calibration split but alive at test time, the prior trades that label's recall for the others' precision. Per-label Platt and beta calibration repair \Sm almost as well and come within $\nNplPlattIsoGap$ and $\nNplBetaIsoGap$ of isotonic on \Nm, but leave \Wm at its raw level ($\nWplPlattPrior$) and the intercept-only shift lowers it to $\nWplOffsetPrior$: the gain on \Wm comes from label-specific non-linear maps that one- and two-parameter families cannot express.

\paragraph{Deployment protocol (\cref{tab:deploy}).} Fitting the calibrators on the validation period (\nnValRows{} rows, the last training months) and evaluating on all \nnTest{} test rows removes the test-period labels from calibration. Under this protocol \Sm goes from $\ndepSraw$ to $\ndepSplIsoPrior$ with per-label isotonic regression and the prior fallback (\ndepSrepairShare\% of its loss against \Nm, whose raw score is $\ndepNraw$), the intercept-only shift returns \ndepSoffsetShare\%, and \Nm changes by $\ndepNprGain$; \ndepSnDeadVal{} labels have no positives in the validation period. The repair therefore does not depend on calibrating with test-period labels; what the test-split protocol adds is the prior shift between training and test months, visible as the difference between the two protocols on \Nm.

\paragraph{MULAN benchmarks.} We retrain one-vs-rest models on \nnMulan{} MULAN datasets~\cite{Tsoumakas2011MULAN} with $w_j\in\{1,\sqrt{r_j},r_j,10r_j\}$, $r_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$, and \nnLearners{} learners: LightGBM in a default and a strongly regularized configuration, XGBoost, $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression with sample weights, and a two-layer MLP with per-label \texttt{pos\_weight}. \Cref{tab:mulan} shows the default LightGBM cells and \cref{app:mulan} every cell. Three regularities hold. (i) For the tree learners raw $\mapk$ falls with the weight magnitude on genbase and enron and, under regularization, on medical, whereas logistic regression and XGBoost on medical gain from weights ($\nmedLogregRawWone\to\nmedLogregRawWr$ and $\nmedXgbRawWone\to\nmedXgbRawWr$ at $w{=}r$); on the \nnMulanModest{} datasets with $\max r<100$ the change at $w{=}r$ is at most $\nmaxDropModest$ and of either sign, in line with the ``class weights are benign'' reports at imbalance ratios below 70~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}. (ii) The what-if prediction is within $0.03$ of the trained weighted model on \nnWhatifClose{} of \nnMulan{} datasets; it under-predicts the loss where the trained model saturates (genbase: $\ngenbaseDefaultWhatifWr$ predicted, $\ngenbaseDefaultRawWr$ trained, distinct scores per label \ngenbaseDistinctWone{} to \ngenbaseDistinctWr) and over-predicts it where regularization shrinks the realized shift (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongWhatifWr$ against $\nenronStrongRawWr$), and where no saturation occurs the analytic inversion recovers the unweighted ranking (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongRawWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nenronStrongRawWr$ at $w{=}r$, $\nenronStrongInvWr$ after inversion). (iii) Where the number of distinct scores per label collapses, the ceiling falls and neither inversion nor calibration returns to the unweighted level (medical, strongly regularized: $\nmedStrongDistinctWone$ to $\nmedStrongDistinctWtenr$ distinct scores and ceiling $\nmedStrongCeilWone$ to $\nmedStrongCeilWtenr$ from $w{=}1$ to $10r$); on medical, where \nmedDeadCal{} of \nmedL{} labels have no calibration positives, the identity fallback loses to the prior by up to $\nmedIdVsPriorMaxGap$. The sweep also contains the negative result the recipe must carry: with few calibration positives, per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback \emph{hurts} an unweighted model. With the default LightGBM at $w{=}1$ it lowers $\mapk$ by more than $0.005$ on \nnHurtDefault{} of \nnMulan{} datasets, and on \nnHurtTauZeroCI{} of them the paired bootstrap interval excludes zero (birds $\nbirdsRawWone\to\nbirdsPlIsoPriorWone$, $\nbirdsCiTauZero$, with a median of \ncalPosMedBirds{} calibration positives per label; medical $\nmedRawWone\to\nmedPlIsoPriorWone$, $\nmedCiTauZero$, with \ncalPosMedMedical; flags $\nflagsCiTauZero$ on \nflagsNtest{} test rows is not significant), and changes it by at most $\nmaxAbsDeltaElsewhere$ elsewhere; across learners the sign varies from dataset to dataset. The median number of calibration positives does not separate the cases cleanly (genbase and enron gain slightly with \ncalPosMedGenbase{} and \ncalPosMedEnron), so no fixed threshold can be recommended. \Cref{tab:tau} tests the selection rule of the recipe instead: on the calibration split alone, \ntauFolds-fold cross-validation chooses among per-label isotonic regression with positives threshold $\tau\in\{\ntauList\}$ (labels with at most $\tau$ calibration positives keep the prior), the shared map, and no calibration. For the default LightGBM at $w{=}1$ the rule keeps the raw scores on birds, medical and flags, where every calibrator hurts or is indistinguishable from raw, keeps the per-label gains on genbase and enron ($\tau=\ngenbaseTauSel$ and $\nenronTauSel$), and on no dataset does the selected candidate lose to the raw model with an interval excluding zero (\nnHurtAfterTau{} of \nnMulan). The rule is not infallible: across all \nnTauCells{} cells (\nnLearners{} learners, two weight settings, \nnMulan{} datasets) the selected calibrator ends more than $0.01$ below raw in \nnTauSelBelowRaw{} cells, against \nnTauZeroBelowRaw{} for the fixed $\tau=0$ rule, and its worst outcome is $\ntauWorstSelMinusRaw$ (\ntauWorstSelCell), where a calibration split of about a hundred rows leaves the inner folds too small to see that no calibrator beats the raw scores. The what-if prediction at $w{=}r$ is within its paired interval of the trained model on \nnWhatifCiCoversZero{} of \nnMulan{} datasets.

\paragraph{Leaf saturation.} Single decision trees with \texttt{class\_weight}$=\{1{:}w\}$ have leaf values equal to the weighted class frequencies, so the saturation share computed from each leaf's $(n_+,n_-)$ and $w$ equals the measured share of predictions within $10^{-3}$ of one by construction; \cref{app:leaf} reports this implementation check and the LightGBM sweep across \texttt{min\_child\_samples} and $w\in\{1,r,10r,100r\}$. On these small datasets the saturated share stays below \nleafLgbmMaxSat\% and the ceiling moves only where the number of distinct scores collapses (medical, \texttt{min\_child\_samples}$=50$: ceiling $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWhundred$ at $100r$). The Santander weights ($w_j$ up to \nwMax) lie far beyond this sweep, which is where the ceiling falls below the unweighted raw score.

\paragraph{Synthetic study.} With known marginals (\cref{app:synthetic}) a realizable learner (logistic regression) attains the Bayes optimum unweighted ($\nsynLRrawDeZero$ against $\nsynTrueD$), weights degrade the ranking monotonically in the spread of $\ln w_j$, and the analytic inversion restores the optimum exactly ($\nsynLRinvD$): \cref{prop:odds} is the whole story. LightGBM fails to invert at both tree counts we tried (a 30-tree, 4-leaf model: $\nsynSmallInvD$; a 300-tree, 31-leaf model: $\nsynLargeInvD$), with \nsynSmallSatD\% and \nsynLargeSatD\% of cells saturated and in-sample ceilings intact ($\nsynSmallCeilD$, $\nsynLargeCeilD$), whereas XGBoost, also a boosted tree, saturates no cell and inverts to $\nsynXgbInvD$, and the MLP inverts to $\nsynMlpInvD$. Capacity is therefore not the deciding factor; the two libraries differ in how far a leaf may move under a large weight (XGBoost's defaults bound the leaf step with $\lambda=1$ and \texttt{min\_child\_weight}$=1$ on the weighted Hessian, LightGBM's \texttt{min\_sum\_hessian\_in\_leaf} is $10^{-3}$ with no $\ell_2$ penalty), and we did not isolate which setting matters. The study reproduces the odds shift, its exact inversion and its failure under saturation; it does not reproduce a ceiling loss of the Santander size, because even where a quarter of the cells saturate the ceiling moves by about $0.01$.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Consistency and top-$K$.} One-vs-rest surrogates are consistent for the rank loss~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate} and, with a proper loss, for precision@$k$~\cite{Menon2019Reductions}; multi-label metrics decompose into per-label decisions on the marginals~\cite{Koyejo2015Consistent}, and the precision@$k$ regret of a plug-in ranker is bounded by its marginal error~\cite{Wydmuch2018PLT}. Propensity-scored metrics weight labels deliberately~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Wydmuch2021PSPLT,Schultheis2023GTU}; \cref{cor:odds}(c) shows that training weights approximate that ranking implicitly. An instance-level weight is constant within a row and rank-neutral; a label-level weight is not.

\paragraph{Imbalance corrections and calibration.} Elkan's identity~\cite{Elkan2001} and the prior-shift correction of~\cite{Saerens2002} give the odds-shift map, which logit adjustment applies post hoc in long-tailed learning~\cite{Menon2021LogitAdjust}; the same prior correction, combined with calibration, is the label-shift adaptation of~\cite{Lipton2018LabelShift,Alexandari2020MLLS}, of which our label-free prevalence-matching shift is the per-label special case. The long-tailed recognition literature reached ``adjust after unweighted training'' for classification: decoupling the classifier from the representation~\cite{Kang2020Decoupling} beats class-balanced~\cite{Cui2019ClassBalanced}, margin~\cite{Cao2019LDAM} and focal~\cite{Lin2017Focal} losses, and threshold moving is the classical cost-sensitive alternative to re-weighting~\cite{Sheng2006Thresholding,He2009Imbalanced}; these rank classes within one softmax, whereas we rank labels across independent one-vs-rest models, where the per-label weight is the distortion. Probability estimates under imbalance corrections are unreliable~\cite{Wallace2012}, undersampling is corrected by an odds shift~\cite{DalPozzolo2015}, class-weighted models can be inverted analytically~\cite{Caplin2022ClassWeights}, and imbalance corrections harm calibration in clinical models without improving discrimination~\cite{VandenGoorbergh2022}; a recent tree-ensemble study at imbalance ratios up to 70 finds class weights benign for calibration error and Platt or isotonic recalibration sufficient~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}, which our modest-imbalance MULAN results confirm, and importance weights are known to lose their effect on learners that can fit the weighted objective~\cite{Byrd2019}. The XGBoost documentation recommends $n_-/n_+$ and warns about probabilities~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; class-balanced losses for GBDT and long-tailed multi-label vision~\cite{Luo2024GBDTImb,Wu2020DBLoss}, classical post-hoc calibration~\cite{Zadrozny2002,NiculescuMizil2005,Guo2017Calibration}, and calibrator selection and benchmarks~\cite{Abdelrahman2025SmartCal,Berta2026CalArena} optimize calibration error, not ranking. None measures the cross-label consequence of label-specific weights or the saturation regime.

\paragraph{Calibration versus ranking.} Shared class-wise calibration recovers the top-5 accuracy lost by independent per-class maps on ImageNet~\cite{Patel2021IMax}; intra-order-preserving maps, Mix-n-Match and Meta-Cal are rank-preserving multi-class calibrators~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder,Zhang2020MixNMatch,Ma2021MetaCal}, Dirichlet calibration is not~\cite{Kull2019Dirichlet}, and the rate at which calibrators change the top-1 prediction has been quantified~\cite{Kim2026Confidence}. In multi-label and extreme classification a shared monotone map keeps precision@$k$ untouched and per-label calibration is deferred to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}; label-wise monotone maps serve reliability reranking~\cite{Tae2026Reranking}, group-wise calibrators shrunk toward a global map are analysed in~\cite{Lavi2025Clustered}, per-class residual offsets are Bayes-optimal for reranking when the distortion is class-separable~\cite{Wang2026BeyondLA}, and normalization-aware, tag-marginal and utility-aware calibration address neighbouring settings~\cite{Arad2025NAIso,Kranzlein2021Marginal,Hegazy2025Utility}. Recommender systems calibrate per rank group, learn monotone layers that keep a ranker's order, correct sampling bias by an additive logit term, and face maximization bias when selected items are evaluated~\cite{Sato2024TopN,Bai2025UnconstrainedMono,Cheng2026IsotonicLayer,Yi2019SamplingBias,Fan2023CalibMatters}; calibration of a distribution over rankings is formalized in~\cite{Thies2026CalibLR}, top-$K$ ranking measures are related in~\cite{Wang2024TKPR}, and two homonyms are unrelated to probability calibration: ``calibrated recommendations''~\cite{Steck2018CalibratedRec}, which matches the genre distribution of a list to the user's history, and ``calibrated label ranking''~\cite{Furnkranz2008CLR}. Relative to this line our contribution is the source of the label-wise distortion (training weights), the what-if bound on its odds-shift part, its saturation regime, and the role of the dead-label fallback.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Recipe.} Estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss; if imbalance makes optimization hard, prefer a common weight (rank-neutral by \cref{cor:odds}(a)) or, when label-specific weights are kept, cap the leaf step (\texttt{max\_delta\_step}$=2$ returned most of the loss at training time in \cref{tab:mds}) and still calibrate per label. Calibrate on a held-out split from the training period, never from the evaluation period. Map every label with at most $\tau$ calibration positives to the prior rather than the identity, and choose $\tau$, per-label versus shared, and whether to calibrate at all, by cross-validation inside the calibration split (\cref{tab:tau}): the candidates are cheap, the objective is the deployed metric, and the rule never used test labels. When the calibration split is small the inner folds cannot expose the harm of per-label maps (birds in \cref{tab:tau}); the shared map is then the safe choice for an unweighted model. On Santander, per-label maps beat the shared map on the unweighted model down to a calibration split of \ncalsizeSmallestNcalPlWins{} rows (median \ncalsizeSmallestMedPlWins{} positives per label) and lose below it, whereas for the weighted model per-label maps win at every size because a shared map cannot undo a per-label distortion (\cref{tab:calsize}). If a utility- or propensity-weighted ranking is wanted, multiply calibrated marginals by the utilities at decision time. Without labels, the share of cells at exactly $1.0$ and the number of distinct scores per label flag saturation and predict that the analytic inversion will fail, though not how much top-$K$ is lost.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The large-scale evidence is one benchmark with 24 labels and one weighted configuration ($w_j=n_-/n_+$, up to \nwMax); the MULAN datasets are small, and neural multi-label models with \texttt{pos\_weight} are covered only by the two-layer MLP of the sweep. Boosted trees are the main learner family; the saturation lemma is stated for trees, and the logistic-regression and MLP results show only that the odds shift is learner-agnostic. The oracle ceiling is an empirical reference, not a bound on all post-hoc procedures, and row-dependent calibrators~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} are outside the separable class. Per-label calibration needs calibration positives; no threshold in the median number of calibration positives separates the harmful from the harmless cases, and the cross-validated selection of \cref{tab:tau} fails on the smallest calibration split, where the shared map has to be chosen by rule rather than by data. The test-split protocol calibrates on rows of the test period and absorbs the prior shift between training and test months; the deployment protocol of \cref{tab:deploy} removes that advantage and is the one to expect in practice. The label-free prevalence-matching shift is infeasible for \nnCappedShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels and is not proposed as a repair. The \texttt{max\_delta\_step} sweep covers two values on one dataset; it shows that a cap removes saturation and most of the raw loss while the analytic inversion still over-corrects, not that any cap makes the inversion exact, and it does not tune the cap.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} Per-label class weights change the target of one-vs-rest training from the marginal to a weighted odds, and on a large recommendation benchmark, for two LightGBM models that differ only in the weights, the textbook odds shift is the minor part of the resulting top-$K$ loss; the major part is a per-label monotone distortion, a realized shift that differs from $\ln w_j$ with saturation ties above the calibration ceiling, which the analytic inversion cannot undo. Per-label calibration with a prior fallback undoes it up to the small residue above the in-sample ceiling, under a deployment protocol as well as under test-split calibration, and the fallback, not the calibrator, decides the sign. For LightGBM with the recommended weights and a per-row ranking, reweighting is the wrong tool; unweighted estimation followed by calibration selected on the calibration split, with the right fallback, is the right one.

\section*{Reproducibility}
All scores, calibrators, tables and figures are produced by the \texttt{code/} and \texttt{paper/} directories of the repository released with this paper (\url{https://github.com/souldrive7/dont-reweight-calibrate}), from fixed prediction arrays (SHA-256 recorded in the result files; the arrays are regenerated from the public Kaggle data by the released training script) and the public MULAN ARFF files (content hashes recorded). The matched Santander pair shares the feature pipeline, the time split and every LightGBM argument except the weight; the configuration of every run is recorded in its metadata. The synthetic generator, the leaf-saturation check, the cross-validated selection and the bootstrap use fixed seeds, and the dead-label policy is a named argument of every calibrator.

\section{Shared and distinct separable maps}
\label{app:proof}
\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:sep}
Let $g_1,\dots,g_L$ be non-decreasing maps on a common interval $I$. (a) If $g_1=\dots=g_L$, the separable calibrator never creates a strict inversion: $s_{ij}>s_{ik}$ implies $\tilde s_{ij}\ge\tilde s_{ik}$, with equality only when both scores fall in the same plateau of the shared map. (b) If the maps are continuous and $g_j(a)\neq g_k(a)$ for some interior $a\in I$ and some $j\neq k$, there is a score vector whose strict within-row order is inverted.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(a) is monotonicity. (b) Say $g_j(a)<g_k(a)$. By continuity of $g_j$ there is $b>a$ in $I$ with $g_j(b)<g_k(a)$; the row with $s_{ij}=b>a=s_{ik}$ has $\tilde s_{ij}<\tilde s_{ik}$. If no such $b$ exists because $a$ is the right endpoint, use continuity of $g_k$ to pick $b<a$ with $g_k(b)>g_j(a)$ and the row $s_{ik}=b<a=s_{ij}$.
\end{proof}

\section{Synthetic study with known marginals}
\label{app:synthetic}
\Cref{tab:synthetic} lists every cell of the synthetic study (settings in the caption); the text of \cref{sec:dose} quotes the $D=3$, $e=1$ rows.
\begin{table*}[p]
\caption{Synthetic multi-label data with known marginals ($L=\nsynL$, $n=\nsynN$ rows for training and test, \nsynSeeds{} seeds, $\mathrm{MAP}@\nsynK$). Prevalences span $10^{-D}$ to $0.3$; weights are $w_j=r_j^{e}$. Ranking by the true marginals is the Bayes optimum. Logistic regression is the realizable learner; LGBM-S is LightGBM with 30 trees and 4 leaves, LGBM-L with 300 trees and 31 leaves; XGBoost (200 trees, depth 5) and a two-layer MLP are the other learners. Both LightGBM sizes fail to invert once cells saturate; XGBoost saturates nothing and inverts. Where the inversion fails, the realized shift is no longer the constant $\ln w_j$ under which a per-label offset is Bayes-optimal~\cite{Wang2026BeyondLA}, but the distortion remains per-label monotone.}
